---
title: "The metrics"
subtitle: "What counts as right, and why each number exists"
---

{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}

Every score here is computed by a deterministic scorer: no model judges another. An answer is parsed
into a list of calls, `{name, arguments}`, and compared with the gold calls.

| Metric | What it measures | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| `parse_ok` | the answer parses as JSON calls | separates "wrote broken JSON" from "called the wrong thing" |
| **`exact`** | the same calls as gold, in any order (`5 == 5.0`, `true != 1`) | the headline: a call is right or it isn't |
| `lenient_exact` | `exact`, but ignoring optional arguments at their default, on either side | gold writes some defaults out and leaves others out; by the tool spec both are the same call |
| `names` | the right functions, each the right number of times | function choice, apart from values |
| `arg_f1` | F1 over `(function, argument, value)` triples | partial credit, to see how wrong a wrong answer is |

::: {.column-margin}
The scorer and its rules: [the README](https://github.com/joaomigueloliveira/qwen-function-calling-distillation#task).
:::

## Strict and lenient

Strict exact is the headline, because it is the one a user would care about: the right calls with
the right values. But on the `{python} defaults_rows` test-clean rows where gold and a model differ
only by an optional argument at its default, strict exact rewards guessing xLAM's habit, not calling
tools well. Lenient exact is reported beside it, and every claim on xLAM is checked under both
([what the methods copy](../results.qmd#what-the-methods-copy)).

## Parsing

A model may wrap its JSON in a code fence; then only the fence's contents are read. Without a fence,
any text around the JSON fails, since a tool-calling system would reject it too. Answers that span
several lines parse like any other. Reasoning blocks are removed first, though thinking is off for
every model here.

## Slices

Every score is also broken down by **call pattern** (one call, several, the same call in parallel),
by **distractor tools** (how many offered tools the answer doesn't use) and by **argument source**
(whether every value is written in the query). A slice is reported on its own only with at least 300
rows; smaller ones are flagged.

## Intervals

Every score comes with a 95% Wilson interval. On `{python} n(splits["test-clean"])` rows, a score
near 80% carries about ±2 points; a comparison between two models on the same rows is tighter, and
is made with a paired test ([comparing methods](comparing.qmd)).

On [BFCL](../data/bfcl.qmd), where each argument has a list of acceptable values, `exact` uses the
same strict comparison and there is no lenient version: BFCL already marks which arguments may be
left out.
